title: Structural Geology
summary: Folds, faults, joints and unconformities — how rocks deform and how to read them in the field.

blocks.title: Structural Geology
blocks.body: The branch of geology that deals with the study of the architecture of the Earth's crust — rock deformation, origin, and mechanism of geological structures such as folds, faults, joints, and unconformities.

blocks.title: Stress
blocks.body: Stress is the pressure applied to rocks, expressed as **force per unit area (F/A)**.

blocks.title: Types of Stress
items: **Lithostatic stress:** Equal pressure exerted on rocks from all directions due to the weight of overlying rocks. Similar to hydrostatic stress.
**Directional/Differential stress:** Unequal stress due to tectonic forces. Three types: (i) Tensional stress (stretching/extension), (ii) Compressional stress (squeezing), (iii) Shearing stress.

blocks.title: Strain
blocks.body: Strain is the **deformation of rocks in response to stress**.

blocks.title: Types of Deformation
items: **Elastic deformation:** For small directional stresses (less than yield strength), rock deforms like a spring (Hooke's Law). Deformation is **not permanent** — rock returns to original shape when stress is released.
**Plastic deformation:** When differential stress exceeds yield strength, rock flows permanently. Occurs in the lower continental crust and mantle.
**Brittle deformation:** Near the Earth's surface, if differential stress exceeds yield strength, rock **fractures or fails** with development of a weak zone/plane.
**Ductile deformation:** At depths greater than **10 km**, enormous lithostatic stress and high temperature make rock softer, less brittle and more malleable, preventing fracture.

blocks.title: Outcrop
blocks.body: The exposure of solid rock on the Earth's surface.

blocks.title: Attitude of Beds
blocks.body: The simplest form of deformation is **tilting of initially horizontal sedimentary beds**. The position of the bed on the ground surface is expressed as its **attitude**, quantified by Strike and Dip.

blocks.title: Strike
blocks.body: The direction of a line formed by the **intersection of a horizontal plane with an inclined bedding plane**. It is the direction of the line of intersection of a geological feature with a horizontal plane.

blocks.title: Dip
blocks.body: The **angle of inclination** of a rock bed relative to the horizontal plane. Measured in a plane **perpendicular to the strike direction**. Expressed in degrees (0°–90°).

blocks.title: True Dip
blocks.body: The **maximum angle of inclination** of a bed, measured perpendicular to the strike direction. True dip is always **greater than or equal to** apparent dip.

blocks.title: Apparent Dip
blocks.body: The angle of inclination of a bed measured in **any direction other than perpendicular to the strike**. Apparent dip is always **less than** true dip. It is zero parallel to strike and increases to equal true dip when measured perpendicular to strike.

blocks.title: Orientation Table
blocks.body: **Horizontal bed:** Strike absent, Dip absent, Dip angle = 0°. **Vertical bed:** Strike present, Dip absent, Dip angle = 90°. **Inclined bed:** Strike present, Dip present, Dip angle >0° and <90°.

blocks.title: Brunton Compass
blocks.body: A **Brunton Pocket Transit** is a precision compass used to measure **strike and dip** of geological features. It uses the Earth's magnetic field and can be adjusted for declination angle. Strike is measured by leveling the compass along the plane; dip is measured by laying the compass perpendicular to strike and using the clinometer.

blocks.title: Fold
blocks.body: A wave-like **bend or curve** formed in rock strata due to **compressive forces**. Folds may occur singly, isolated, or as extensive fold trains of different sizes.

blocks.title: Parts of a Fold
items: **Axial plane:** An imaginary plane that divides the fold into two halves as symmetrically as possible.
**Axis/Hinge:** An imaginary line along which the bedding plane has suffered **maximum bending or curvature**. It may or may not coincide with the axial plane.
**Crest:** The convex or up-arched (highest) part of the fold.
**Trough:** The concave or down-arched (lowest) part of the fold.
**Limbs/Flanks:** The sides of a fold. In a series of folds, the part between the crest of one fold and the trough of the adjacent fold.

blocks.title: Anticline
blocks.body: A fold that is **convex upward**. The limbs dip **away from each other** with reference to its axial plane. The **oldest beds** occur towards the core or centre of curvature.

blocks.title: Syncline
blocks.body: A fold that is **convex downward** (opposite of anticline). The limbs dip **towards each other** with reference to its axial plane. The **youngest beds** occur towards the core or centre of curvature.

blocks.title: Symmetrical Fold
blocks.body: A fold in which the **axial plane is vertical** and the two limbs dip at the **same angle** in opposite directions. Formed when compressive forces from both sides are **equal** (P₁ = P₂). One half is the mirror image of the other.

blocks.title: Asymmetrical Fold
blocks.body: A fold in which the **axial plane is inclined** and the two limbs dip at **different angles** on either side of the axial plane. Formed when compressive forces from two sides are **unequal** (P₁ > P₂).

blocks.title: Overturned Fold
blocks.body: A fold in which the axial plane is **highly inclined** and both limbs dip in the **same direction** at different angles. Formed when compressive force is very high on one side (P₁ ≫ P₂).

blocks.title: Recumbent Fold
blocks.body: A fold in which the axial plane is **horizontal or nearly horizontal** (dip angle approximately 0°). Formed when compressive force is extremely high on one side.

blocks.title: Isoclinal Fold
blocks.body: A fold in which the limbs dip at the **same angle in the same direction** — the limbs are parallel to each other. The axial plane is inclined.

blocks.title: Fan Fold
blocks.body: A fold in which the limbs dip **towards each other** (synclinal fan fold) or **away from each other** (anticlinal fan fold), resembling a fan. Crests and troughs are broad and rounded.

blocks.title: Open and Closed Fold
blocks.body: **Open Fold:** Angle between limbs is **obtuse** (>90° but <180°). Bed thickness remains uniform. **Closed Fold:** Angle between limbs is **acute** (<90°). Beds are thicker at the hinge and thinner at the limbs.

blocks.title: Chevron Fold
blocks.body: Folds with **sharp, angular hinges** and **straight limbs**.

blocks.title: Box Fold
blocks.body: A fold with a **flat-topped crest** and two **vertical/steep limbs**, forming a box-like shape.

blocks.title: Monoclinal Fold
blocks.body: A fold with a **local steepening** in horizontal or gently dipping strata. Only **one limb** is inclined.

blocks.title: Anticlinorium and Synclinorium
blocks.body: **Anticlinorium:** A large anticlinal structure consisting of a series of smaller folds (anticlines and synclines) superimposed on it. **Synclinorium:** A large synclinal structure consisting of a series of smaller folds superimposed on it.

blocks.title: Plunging and Non-plunging Fold
blocks.body: **Plunging fold:** A fold whose axis is **inclined to the horizontal plane**. The angle of inclination is the plunge angle. **Non-plunging fold:** A fold whose axis is **horizontal** (plunge angle = 0°).

blocks.title: Dome and Basin
blocks.body: **Dome (Pericline):** A double-folded structure where beds dip **away from a central point** in all directions, forming an inverted bowl shape. **Basin:** Beds dip **towards a central point** from all directions, forming a bowl shape.

blocks.title: Significance of Folds
items: **Mountain building:** Folds create valleys, hills, and mountain ranges. The Himalayas are fold mountains.
**Groundwater occurrence:** Synclines provide favourable conditions for groundwater; artesian springs and wells owe their origin to synclinal structures.
**Oil and Gas deposits:** Anticlinal folds serve as good structural traps for oil and gas deposits.

blocks.title: Mumbai High Field
blocks.body: Mumbai High (Bombay High) is an offshore oilfield in the Arabian Sea, ~160 km west of Mumbai coast. Discovered in 1974. The structure is a **north-northwest to south-southeast trending doubly plunging anticline** with a faulted east limb, 65 km long and 23 km wide. Operated by ONGC.

blocks.title: Fault
blocks.body: A **planar fracture** in a volume of rock across which there has been **significant displacement** along the fracture as a result of Earth movements. Energy release associated with rapid movement on active faults is the main cause of **earthquakes**.

blocks.title: Parts of a Fault
items: **Fault Plane:** The fracture plane along which displacement occurs. Its intersection with the horizontal plane gives the **strike** of the fault.
**Footwall:** The rock block that lies **below** the fault plane.
**Hanging wall:** The rock block that lies **above** the fault plane.
**Slip/Displacement:** The relative movement of blocks along the fault plane. Total displacement is the **net slip** (may be strike-slip, dip-slip, or both).
**Heave:** The **horizontal** component of displacement.
**Throw:** The **vertical** component of displacement.

blocks.title: Normal Fault
blocks.body: A fault in which the **hanging wall moves downward** relative to the footwall. Also called **gravity fault**. Results from **tensional forces** (stretching/extension). Lengthening of the crust occurs.

blocks.title: Normal fault dip angle
blocks.body: **Confirm with Vandana Miss.** There are two answers here: the teacher's notes do not specify a particular dip angle range for normal faults (or suggest 0°-45°), while the textbook states normal faults have dips **greater than 45°** (p.49). Leave this for the students to ask the teacher.

blocks.title: Reverse Fault
blocks.body: A fault in which the **hanging wall moves upward** relative to the footwall. Results from **compressional forces**. Shortening of the crust occurs.

blocks.title: Reverse Fault vs Thrust Fault
blocks.body: **Confirm with Vandana Miss.** There are two answers here: the teacher's notes treat **reverse fault and thrust fault as synonymous**, while the textbook **splits** them (reverse faults have dips **>45°**, thrust faults have dips **<45°**). Leave this for the students to ask the teacher.

blocks.title: Thrust Fault (Textbook detail)
blocks.body: According to the textbook, a thrust fault is a **special case of reverse fault** characterised by **low dip angles (less than 45°)**.

blocks.title: Strike-Slip Fault
blocks.body: A fault in which the blocks slide past each other along the **direction of strike**. Displacement is **horizontal**, parallel to the strike of the fault plane. Also called **lateral fault, trans-current fault, wrench fault, or tear fault**.

blocks.title: Dip-Slip Fault
blocks.body: A fault in which the displacement is **vertical/inclined**, parallel to the dip of the fault plane.

blocks.title: Oblique-Slip Fault
blocks.body: A fault in which displacement has **both horizontal (strike) and vertical (dip) components**.

blocks.title: Step Faults
blocks.body: A series of **parallel normal faults** occurring at regular intervals, with blocks displaced in the same direction, giving a **step-like appearance**.

blocks.title: Horst and Graben
blocks.body: **Horst:** When normal faults with mutually diverging/converging fault planes occur, the **central block is displaced upward** relative to adjacent blocks. Forms **block mountains**. **Graben:** The **central block is displaced downward** relative to adjacent blocks. Forms **rift valleys**.

blocks.title: Additional Fault Classifications (Notes)
items: **Strike Fault:** Fault plane strike is parallel to the strike of inclined beds.
**Dip Fault:** Fault plane strike is parallel to the dip direction of inclined beds.
**Oblique Fault:** Fault plane strike is neither parallel to strike nor dip of the bedding plane.
**Bedding Fault:** Fault plane is parallel to the bedding plane.
**Radial Fault:** Multiple fault lines diverging from a central point.

blocks.title: Significance of Faults
items: Faults cause damage to rocks — real hazards in **mining and engineering works**.
Fault breccia and fault gouge have low strength — **poor foundation materials**.
**Earthquakes and landslides** are triggered by faults.
Knowledge of faults helps in proper designing of large civil structures (dams, tunnels).
Many fault zones are suitable sites for **mineralization** (gold, silver, copper).
Faults may create **lakes, swamps, hot water springs** (sources of geothermal energy).
Some fault zones form potential **oil traps**.

blocks.title: Joint
blocks.body: A **fracture or crack** in a rock along which there has been **little to no displacement**. Joints divide rocks into blocks. Unlike faults, joints have **no significant displacement** along the fracture plane.

blocks.title: Joint vs Fault
blocks.body: **Key difference:** Fault has displacement; Joint has **no displacement**. Both are fractures in rock.

blocks.title: Genetic Classification of Joints (Notes)
items: **Tensional Joint:** Formed due to pulling apart forces (tension).
**Compressional Joint:** Formed due to pushing together forces (compression).
**Shear Joint:** Formed due to sliding/tearing forces (shear).

blocks.title: Geometric Classification of Joints
items: **Strike Joint:** Joint runs **parallel to the strike** of the inclined bedding plane.
**Dip Joint:** Joint runs **parallel to the dip direction** of the inclined bedding plane.
**Diagonal/Oblique Joint:** Joint runs at an **angle oblique** to both strike and dip of the bedding plane.
**Bedding Joint:** Joint is **parallel to the bedding plane**.

blocks.title: Columnar Joints
blocks.body: Sets of intersecting closely spaced fractures formed as rock **cools and contracts**. Cracks develop vertically, dividing rock into **hexagonal or pentagonal columns**. Most commonly observed in **basalt**. Columns can vary from a few centimetres to few metres in diameter, and can be several hundred metres in height. Number of sides can vary from **3 to 8**.

blocks.title: Columnar Joint Examples
blocks.body: Naldurga Fort (Osmanabad), Panhala Fort (Kolhapur), **Gilbert Hill (Mumbai)**, St. Mary's Island (Malpe, Udupi, Karnataka). Columnar joints in **rhyolite** at Utan in Thane district.

blocks.title: Mural (Cuboidal) Joint
blocks.body: A set of **three mutually perpendicular joints** (two vertical and one horizontal) that divide rock into **cuboidal blocks**. Commonly seen in **granites**.

blocks.title: Sheet Joint
blocks.body: Fractures that are essentially **horizontal and concentric**, cutting rock into **sheet or slab-like forms**. Commonly seen in plutonic igneous rocks (e.g., granite domes).

blocks.title: Significance of Joints
items: Split rocks into blocks, **reducing competence** of rock mass.
Increase **porosity and permeability**, making rocks susceptible to quick decay and weathering.
Increase the **groundwater potential** in any area.
Minerals are exposed on the surface through joint planes.
Groundwater is exposed as **springs** through joint planes.
Different shapes of rock weathering (columnar, cuboidal) are due to joint planes.
Joints can be improved by suitable methods such as **cement grouting or plugging**.

blocks.title: Unconformity
blocks.body: A **surface of erosion or non-deposition** separating younger strata from older rocks, representing a **gap in the geologic record**. A buried erosional surface where an expected age of rock layers is missing due to erosion. This gap in time is called a **hiatus**.

blocks.title: Conformable vs Unconformable Series
blocks.body: **Conformable series:** An unbroken sequence of sedimentary beds deposited one above another **without any tectonic disturbance**, weathering, or erosion. All beds have the same strike, dip direction, and dip amount. **Unconformable series:** A sequence where older beds have undergone tectonic movement, weathering, or erosion, followed by deposition of a younger series.

blocks.title: Angular Unconformity
blocks.body: An unconformity where older sedimentary beds are **inclined/tilted at an angle**, while younger beds above are **horizontal or less tilted**. The older and younger beds are **not mutually parallel**.

blocks.title: Formation of Angular Unconformity
items: Deposition and stratification of older sediments to form the older series.
Upliftment and tilting/folding of the older beds.
Weathering and erosion of the tilted beds to form an eroded surface.
Deposition of a younger series of sediments on top of the eroded surface.

blocks.title: Hutton's Angular Unconformity
blocks.body: At **Siccar Point**, 345-million-year-old Devonian Old Red Sandstone overlies 425-million-year-old Silurian greywacke. James Hutton first recognized angular unconformity.

blocks.title: Disconformity (Parallel Unconformity)
blocks.body: An unconformity where the older and younger series are **parallel to each other**, both in horizontal position (dip angle = 0°). It is an **erosional contact** that separates parallel bedding planes. Hard to recognize — often discovered through **fossil study**. May result from erosion or non-deposition.

blocks.title: Formation of Disconformity
items: Deposition of sediments to form the older series.
Upliftment of the older series **without tilting**.
Erosion of the upper/youngest layers of the older series.
Deposition of beds of the younger series.

blocks.title: Nonconformity
blocks.body: An unconformity in which the underlying older formation is **igneous or metamorphic rock** and the overlying younger formation is **sedimentary rock**. Suggests a period of long-term **uplift, weathering, and erosion** to expose the deeper crystalline rock before burial by younger sediments.

blocks.title: Formation of Nonconformity
items: Formation of plutonic igneous or metamorphic rock.
Upliftment of this crystalline basement.
Erosion of the upper layer of the older rock.
Deposition of sedimentary beds of the younger series.

blocks.title: Disconformity Example
blocks.body: Disconformity between sedimentary rocks in **California**, with conglomerate deposited upon an erosion surface on the underlying rocks.

blocks.title: Nonconformity Example
blocks.body: Nonconformity at **Yellowstone Highway, Wyoming**.

blocks.title: Significance of Unconformities
items: Represents a **gap/break in deposition** of beds and a record of a gap in time.
Useful for **subdividing stratigraphic units**, determining timing of tectonic activity, correlating stratigraphic boundaries, interpreting sea-level changes.
Produces **oil traps and aquifers** in certain situations.
Helps in visualizing and reconstructing **palaeogeography** of a region.
Favourable sites for **mineralization** (uranium, aluminium, phosphates, gold).
Forms a **weak zone** affecting site conditions for engineering works.
Tells the **relative age** of rock layers.

blocks.title: Applications of Structural Geology
items: **Engineering geology and geotechnology:** Construction of bridges, dams, power plants, highways, airports, building foundations.
**Environmental geology:** Land use planning, earthquake hazard, volcanic hazard, distribution of groundwater.
**Petroleum and mining geology:** Geometric techniques, projection of faults, geologic contacts, trends of regional processes controlling mineral and hydrocarbon concentration.

questions.prompt: The direction of a line formed due to intersection of an inclined bed with the horizontal plane is called:
questions.explanation: Strike is the direction of the line formed by the intersection of an inclined bedding plane with a horizontal plane. Dip is the angle of inclination, hade is the complement of dip, and heave is horizontal fault displacement.

questions.prompt: An imaginary plane that divides the fold into two equal halves is known as:
questions.explanation: The axial plane is the imaginary plane that divides a fold as symmetrically as possible. The axis is a line, the fault plane relates to faults, and the crest is the highest point.

questions.prompt: An anticline is a fold that is:

options.text: Convex upwards and has its youngest bed at the core
Convex downwards and has its youngest bed at the core
Convex downwards and has its oldest bed at the core
Convex upwards and has its oldest bed at the core

questions.explanation: An anticline is convex upward and the oldest beds are at the core because erosion exposes progressively older layers. A syncline is convex downward with youngest beds at the core.

questions.prompt: In an asymmetrical syncline, the two limbs:

options.text: Dip towards each other by the same angle
Dip away from each other by the same angle
Dip towards each other by different angles
Dip away from each other by different angles

questions.explanation: In a syncline, limbs dip towards each other. In an asymmetrical fold, the angles are different. So limbs dip towards each other by different angles.

questions.prompt: A fracture along which there has been no slipping or displacement of rocks is called a:
questions.explanation: A joint is a fracture with no displacement. A fault has displacement. An unconformity is a gap in deposition. A fold is a bend.

questions.prompt: A type of fault in which the hanging wall block has been displaced upwards with respect to the footwall block is called:
questions.explanation: In a reverse fault, the hanging wall moves upward due to compression. In a normal fault, the hanging wall moves downward.

questions.prompt: An unconformity in which the older bed is made up of igneous or metamorphic rocks is called:
questions.explanation: In a nonconformity, the underlying formation is igneous or metamorphic rock, overlain by sedimentary rock.

questions.prompt: Cracks or fractures in the Earth's crust along which there has been slipping or displacement of rocks are called:
questions.explanation: Faults are fractures with significant displacement. Joints have no displacement. Folds are bends. Unconformities are gaps in deposition.

questions.prompt: Wavy undulations or bends developed in rocks are called:
questions.explanation: Folds are wave-like bends formed in rock strata due to compressive forces.

questions.prompt: A set of parallel normal faults which occur at regular intervals gives rise to a ______ fault.
questions.explanation: Step faults are formed when parallel normal faults occur at regular intervals, creating a staircase pattern.

questions.prompt: Surface of erosion or non-deposition that separates two series of beds is termed as:
questions.explanation: An unconformity is a surface of erosion or non-deposition representing a gap in the geologic record.

questions.prompt: A joint which is parallel to the dip direction of adjacent beds is called a ______ joint.
questions.explanation: A dip joint runs parallel to the dip direction. Strike joint is parallel to strike, diagonal is oblique, bedding is parallel to the bedding plane.

questions.prompt: In a symmetrical syncline, the two limbs:

options.text: Dip towards each other by the same angle
Dip away from each other by different angles
Dip towards each other by different angles
Dip away from each other by the same angle

questions.explanation: Syncline = limbs dip towards each other. Symmetrical = same angle. Therefore: dip towards each other by the same angle.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a reverse fault is correct?

options.text: A reverse fault is a result of tensional forces in which hanging wall is displaced downwards.
A reverse fault is a result of compressional forces in which footwall is displaced upwards.
A reverse fault is a result of compressional forces in which hanging wall is displaced upwards.
A reverse fault is a result of tensional forces in which footwall is displaced downwards.

questions.explanation: A reverse fault results from compression and the hanging wall moves upward relative to the footwall.

questions.prompt: At Gilbert Hill, Mumbai, columnar joints are well exhibited in ______ rocks.
questions.explanation: Gilbert Hill is a famous example of columnar joints in basalt, formed when Deccan lava cooled and contracted.

questions.prompt: The part between the crest of one fold and the trough of the adjacent fold is its:
questions.explanation: The limb is the side of a fold — the part between the crest of one fold and the trough of the adjacent fold.

questions.prompt: Match the following fault-related terms:
questions.explanation: Throw is vertical; Heave is horizontal. Normal = HW down; Reverse = HW up.

questions.prompt: Match the following fold-related terms:
questions.explanation: Anticline arches up; Syncline bows down. Symmetrical = equal angles; Asymmetrical = unequal.

questions.prompt: Match the following unconformity-related terms:

pairs.right: Older series not parallel to younger series
Older bed made up of plutonic igneous rocks
Older series parallel to younger series

questions.explanation: Angular = not parallel. Nonconformity = igneous/metamorphic below. Disconformity = parallel beds.

questions.prompt: Match the following terms:

pairs.right: Older and younger beds are not parallel

questions.explanation: Bedding joint follows the bedding plane. Angular unconformity has non-parallel beds. Syncline is concave. Thrust fault has low dip (<45°).

questions.prompt: Enlist and describe the parts of a fold.
questions.answer: The parts of a fold are: (1) **Axial plane** — an imaginary plane dividing the fold symmetrically. (2) **Axis/Hinge** — the line of maximum bending. (3) **Crest** — the highest up-arched part. (4) **Trough** — the lowest down-arched part. (5) **Limbs/Flanks** — the sides of the fold.
questions.explanation: Draw a labelled diagram showing all five parts. This is a frequently asked question.

questions.prompt: Write a note on an Anticline and draw a labelled diagram.
questions.answer: An anticline is a fold **convex upward** (Greek: opposite inclined). Limbs dip **away from each other**. **Oldest beds** at the core. Diagram labels: axial plane (vertical for symmetrical), left limb, right limb, crest.
questions.explanation: Anticlines are important as structural traps for oil and gas. Oldest beds at core (opposite of syncline).

questions.prompt: What are Symmetrical folds?
questions.answer: Folds with a **vertical axial plane** dividing the fold into mirror-image halves. Both limbs dip at the **same angle**. Forces from both sides are **equal** (P₁ = P₂). Types: Symmetrical Anticline (limbs away, equal) and Symmetrical Syncline (limbs towards, equal).
questions.explanation: Key difference from asymmetrical: vertical axial plane, equal limb angles, equal forces.

questions.prompt: Describe the different parts of a fault with a neatly labelled diagram.
questions.answer: Parts: (1) **Fault Plane** — the fracture surface. (2) **Footwall** — block below fault plane. (3) **Hanging Wall** — block above. (4) **Slip** — the displacement (net, strike, or dip). (5) **Heave** — horizontal component. (6) **Throw** — vertical component. Diagram must label: fault plane, footwall, hanging wall, arrow.
questions.explanation: Teacher-confirmed labels for fault diagrams: fault plane, foot wall, hanging wall, arrow.

questions.prompt: Describe a Thrust fault with a neat diagram.
questions.answer: A thrust fault is a **special case of reverse fault** with **low dip angles (<45°)**. Hanging wall moves upward. Caused by compression. Note: teacher's notes treat reverse and thrust as synonymous.
questions.explanation: Known teacher-textbook conflict. If asked specifically about thrust, mention the textbook's low dip angle distinction.

questions.prompt: What is a Horst and Graben? Draw a suitable diagram.
questions.answer: **Horst:** Central block displaced **upward** between diverging normal faults. Forms **block mountains**. **Graben:** Central block displaced **downward**. Forms **rift valleys**. Both formed by normal faulting (tensional forces).
questions.explanation: Horst = up = block mountain. Graben = down = rift valley.

questions.prompt: What are Strike-slip faults?
questions.answer: Blocks slide past each other along the **direction of strike**. Displacement is **horizontal**. Also called lateral, trans-current, wrench, or tear fault. Types: Left-lateral (sinistral) and Right-lateral (dextral).
questions.explanation: Strike-slip faults are caused by shearing forces.

questions.prompt: Describe and draw a diagram of an Angular unconformity.
questions.answer: Older beds are **inclined/tilted**, younger beds above are **horizontal**. Beds are **not mutually parallel**. Formation: deposition → tilting → erosion → new deposition. Example: Siccar Point.
questions.explanation: The key feature is non-parallel older and younger beds.

questions.prompt: What is a Bedding joint?
questions.answer: A joint (fracture) that is **parallel to the bedding plane** of sedimentary rocks. Develops along the weak planes between successive layers.
questions.explanation: Simplest joint type to identify — follows the bedding plane orientation.

questions.prompt: Write a note on Asymmetrical folds, giving their types with a diagram.
questions.answer: Asymmetrical folds have an **inclined axial plane** with limbs dipping at **different angles**. Unequal forces (P₁ > P₂). Types: Asymmetrical Anticline (limbs away, different angles) and Asymmetrical Syncline (limbs towards, different angles). Progressive types from notes: Overturned (both limbs same direction), Recumbent (horizontal axial plane), Isoclinal (parallel limbs).
questions.explanation: Compare with symmetrical folds: vertical axial plane, equal angles, equal forces.

questions.prompt: Explain the different types of faults with neatly labelled diagrams.
questions.answer: Types: (1) **Normal** — HW down, tension. (2) **Reverse** — HW up, compression, dip >45°. (3) **Thrust** — reverse with dip <45°. (4) **Strike-Slip** — horizontal movement along strike. (5) **Step** — parallel normal faults. (6) **Horst/Graben** — raised/sunken blocks. Each diagram: fault plane, footwall, hanging wall, arrow.
questions.explanation: For 4 marks, draw at least 3 types with labelled diagrams.

questions.prompt: Explain Columnar joints and give an example.
questions.answer: Formed when lava **cools and contracts**. Cracks create **polygonal columns** (3-8 sides, mostly hexagonal). A few cm to metres diameter, hundreds of metres tall. Most common in **basalt**. Examples: Gilbert Hill (Mumbai), Naldurga Fort, Panhala Fort, St. Mary's Island. Rhyolite columns at Utan, Thane.
questions.explanation: Key: cooling and contraction of lava. Gilbert Hill is the most exam-relevant example.

questions.prompt: Describe Disconformity and Nonconformity, giving diagrams of each.
questions.answer: **Disconformity:** Both series **parallel** and sedimentary. Erosional contact. Discovered through fossils. **Nonconformity:** Older formation is **igneous/metamorphic**, younger is sedimentary. Suggests long-term uplift and erosion of crystalline basement.
questions.explanation: Key: disconformity = both sedimentary, parallel. Nonconformity = crystalline basement below.

questions.prompt: What is meant by Strike and Dip of beds? Name the tool used to measure it.
questions.answer: **Strike:** Direction of intersection line of inclined bed with horizontal plane. **Dip:** Angle of inclination perpendicular to strike (0°-90°). **True dip** is maximum (perpendicular to strike). **Apparent dip** is less (any other direction). Tool: **Brunton Compass** (Pocket Transit) or Clinometer Compass.
questions.explanation: Strike = direction, Dip = angle. They are always perpendicular.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a part of a fold?
questions.explanation: Footwall is a part of a fault (block below the fault plane), not a fold. Axial plane, crest, and limb are all parts of a fold.

rows.a: One half is mirror image of other
Hard to recognize; found through fossils

glossary.definition: The branch of geology dealing with rock deformation, origin, and mechanism of geological structures.
Pressure applied to rocks, expressed as force per unit area (F/A).
The deformation of rocks in response to stress.
The exposure of solid rock on the Earth's surface.
Direction of line formed by intersection of a horizontal plane with an inclined bedding plane.
Angle of inclination of a rock bed relative to horizontal, measured perpendicular to strike.
Maximum angle of inclination of a bed, measured perpendicular to the strike direction.
Angle of inclination measured in any direction other than perpendicular to strike. Always less than true dip.
A wave-like bend or curve formed in rock strata due to compressive forces.
An imaginary plane that divides a fold as symmetrically as possible.
A fold convex upward with limbs dipping away from each other. Oldest beds at the core.
A fold convex downward with limbs dipping towards each other. Youngest beds at the core.
A planar fracture in rock across which there has been significant displacement.
The plane along which adjacent blocks are relatively displaced.
The rock block that lies below the fault plane.
The rock block that lies above the fault plane.
Fault where hanging wall moves downward relative to footwall, caused by tensional forces.
Fault where hanging wall moves upward relative to footwall, caused by compressional forces.
Horizontal component of displacement along a fault.
Vertical component of displacement along a fault.
A fracture or crack in rock along which there has been little to no displacement.
Joints formed during cooling of lava, dividing rock into polygonal columns. Most common in basalt.
Surface of erosion or non-deposition separating younger strata from older rocks.
Gap in time represented by an unconformity where expected rock layers are missing.
Unconformity where older beds are tilted/folded while younger beds above are horizontal.
Unconformity where older and younger series are parallel, separated by erosion surface.
Unconformity where older igneous or metamorphic rock is overlain by younger sedimentary rock.
Raised block between normal faults, forming block mountains.
Sunken block between normal faults, forming rift valleys.
